entry: Thunderstorm characterized by a mesocyclone, a deep, persistently rotating updraft. Supercells are the least common thunderstorm type but have the greatest potential to be severe. Often isolated, they can dominate local weather up to 32 km (20 mi) away and usually last 2–4 hours. Low-precipitation supercells are typical of arid climates such as the high plains of the [[United States]]; high-precipitation types occur in moist climates. Only 30% or fewer produce [[Tornado|tornadoes]], but they often bring [[Hail|hail]], torrential rain and strong [[Wind|wind]]. They are most common in the [[Great Plains]] of the United States, known as Tornado Alley.

Person aged 110 or older. About one in 1,000 centenarians reaches this age. A 2010 study found 663 validated supercentenarians, living and dead, with the most in the [[United States]], [[Japan]], England and Wales, [[France]] and [[Italy]], in that order. The earliest supercentenarian accepted by [[Guinness World Records]] is Thomas Peters of the [[Netherlands]], though his age cannot be reliably verified. A study arguing that many validated cases contain errors won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2024.

Large group of smaller [[Galaxy|galaxy]] clusters or galaxy groups, among the largest known structures in the [[Universe]]. The [[Milky Way]] is part of the [[Local Group]], which contains more than 54 galaxies, and of the [[Laniakea Supercluster]], itself within the larger Pisces–Cetus Supercluster Complex. Because of their large size and low density, most superclusters expand with the Hubble expansion, unlike clusters. The observable universe is estimated to contain 10 million superclusters. George Abell first proposed their existence in his 1958 catalog of galaxy clusters, calling them "second-order clusters." Superclusters form filaments, walls and sheets spanning several hundred million to 10 billion light-years, covering more than 5% of the observable universe. The Sloan Great Wall extends up to 1.4 billion light-years.

High-performance [[Computer|computer]] designed for computationally intensive tasks. Supercomputers are used for [[Weather forecasting|weather forecasting]], climate research, oil and gas exploration, molecular modeling, and simulations of aerodynamics and nuclear weapons. Performance is measured in floating-point operations per second (FLOPS). Exascale machines, capable of over 10¹⁸ FLOPS, have existed since 2022. Since November 2017, all of the world's 500 fastest supercomputers have run on [[Linux]]-based operating systems. Supercomputers were introduced in the 1960s; the [[IBM]] 7030 was completed in 1961 for Los Alamos National Laboratory. For several decades the fastest machines were built by Seymour Cray. As of June 2026, LineShine at the National Supercomputing Center in Shenzhen is the world's fastest supercomputer.

Property of certain materials with exactly zero electrical resistance and expelled magnetic fields. Superconductivity was discovered in solid [[Mercury (element)|mercury]] on April 8, 1911, by Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes. Unlike ordinary metals, superconductors drop abruptly to zero resistance below a critical temperature, and a current in a superconducting loop can persist indefinitely. In 1933, Meissner and Ochsenfeld showed that superconductors expel internal magnetic fields, a phenomenon known as the Meissner effect. A theory based on electron pairing was developed in 1957 by [[John Bardeen]], Leon Cooper and John Robert Schrieffer. In 1986, cuprate ceramics were found to superconduct above 35 K; replacing lanthanum with yttrium raised the critical temperature to 92 K, above the boiling point of [[Liquid nitrogen|liquid nitrogen]] (77 K, −196 °C), making liquid nitrogen usable as a refrigerant. Applications include superconducting magnets in [[Magnetic resonance imaging|MRI]] machines and the [[Large Hadron Collider]].

Landmass formed by most or all of Earth's continental blocks, or cratons. Supercontinents assemble and disperse through [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]] over geologic time. By modern definitions none exists today; the closest is the Afro-Eurasian landmass, which covers about 57% of Earth's land area. The most recent, [[Pangaea]], began to break up about 215 million years ago. Earlier, [[Rodinia]] broke apart between about 825 and 750 million years ago. A future supercontinent, Pangaea Proxima, is hypothesized to form within 250 million years.

Property of a fluid with zero [[Viscosity|viscosity]], flowing without loss of kinetic energy. It occurs in the helium isotopes helium-3 and helium-4 when cooled to cryogenic temperatures, and stirring a superfluid creates vortices that rotate indefinitely. Pyotr Kapitsa and, independently, John F. Allen and Don Misener discovered it in helium-4. Lev Landau developed the accepted macroscopic theory in 1941. Superfluidity often co-occurs with [[Bose–Einstein condensate|Bose–Einstein condensation]], though the two are not directly related. In 2005, Wolfgang Ketterle's team at MIT observed quantum vortices in an ultracold gas of lithium-6, a fermionic superfluid.

Type of [[Star|star]] that is among the most massive and luminous. Supergiants occupy the top region of the [[Hertzsprung–Russell diagram]], with absolute visual magnitudes of about −3 to −8 and surface temperatures from about 3,400 K to over 20,000 K. Blue supergiants are the hottest, red supergiants the coolest, and yellow supergiants lie between. The Morgan–Keenan system assigns them luminosity class I. Stars with initial masses above 8–10 solar masses become supergiants after leaving the [[Main sequence|main sequence]], and end as Type II [[Supernova|supernovae]] when their iron cores collapse. [[Betelgeuse]] in [[Orion (constellation)|Orion]] is a well-known red example, and [[Rigel]] is a blue one.

Fictional character with extraordinary powers, typically in a costume, who protects the public and fights crime. Powers may derive from superhuman biology, as with [[Superman]], from advanced technology, as with [[Batman]] or Iron Man, or from magic. Antecedents include mythological figures such as [[Hanuman]] and [[Odysseus]], as well as Heracles, Perseus and English folk heroes such as Robin Hood. The modern genre began in American comic books with Action Comics #1 in 1938 and later spread to films, television, video games, and Japanese manga and anime. During World War II, characters such as [[Captain America]] symbolized Allied resolve. In 1954 Fredric Wertham's critique linked comics to juvenile delinquency, leading to the Comics Code Authority. A 1960s revival came with [[Marvel Comics]] heroes such as [[Spider-Man]] and the X-Men, who grappled with personal flaws.

[[Superhero]] published by [[DC Comics]], created by writer Jerry Siegel and artist Joe Shuster. Superman first appeared in Action Comics #1 on April 18, 1938, and popularized the superhero genre and its conventions. He was the best-selling superhero in American comic books until the 1980s. Born Kal-El on the planet Krypton, he was sent as an infant to [[Earth]] and adopted in Smallville, Kansas, by Jonathan and Martha Kent, who named him Clark Kent. Earth's yellow sun gives him powers far beyond those of humans, including near invulnerability and unassisted flight. Clark works as a reporter for the Daily Planet in Metropolis, and his archenemy is Lex Luthor. The character was created during the [[Great Depression]]. [[Christopher Reeve]] played him in the 1978 film and its sequels.

Largest type of [[Black hole|black hole]], with a mass from hundreds of thousands to billions of times that of the [[Sun]]. Almost every large galaxy has one at its center; the [[Milky Way]]'s is [[Sagittarius A*]]. Accretion of gas onto them powers active galactic nuclei and [[Quasar|quasars]]. The Event Horizon Telescope has imaged two: Sagittarius A* and the black hole at the center of [[Messier 87]], a giant elliptical galaxy. Classically defined as having more than 100,000 solar masses, supermassive black holes have weaker tidal forces at their [[Event horizon|event horizon]] than smaller ones. A person at the horizon of a 10 million solar mass black hole would feel about the same head-to-foot tidal force as on Earth's surface. Because density is inversely proportional to the square of mass, the average density of a supermassive black hole can be less than that of water.

American dark fantasy television series, 2005–2020. Created by Eric Kripke, it ran for 15 seasons, first on The WB and from 2006 on [[The CW]]. Brothers Sam and Dean Winchester hunt ghosts, monsters and other supernatural beings while battling angels and demons to prevent the [[Apocalypse]]. Production was based in [[Vancouver]], British Columbia, and the soundtrack includes "Carry On Wayward Son" by Kansas. Critics called the first five seasons the series' peak, and later seasons drew criticism for repetitive storylines. It was the longest-running fantasy series in American television history.

Phenomena or entities beyond the laws of nature, such as spirits, angels, demons, gods and goddesses. The term emerged in the Middle Ages and did not exist in the ancient world. Many cultures lack concepts that separate the natural from the supernatural. The supernatural features in religious and folkloric contexts, and as an explanation in secular contexts such as [[Superstition|superstition]] and belief in the [[Paranormal|paranormal]]. It also includes claimed abilities such as [[Magic (supernatural)|magic]], telekinesis, levitation, precognition and extrasensory perception. [[Thomas Aquinas]] classified miracles as above, beyond or against nature, sharpening the distinction between nature and miracles.

Principle of linear systems, in which responses to several stimuli combine by addition. The net response to two or more stimuli equals the sum of the responses each would produce alone. A function is linear if it satisfies additivity, F(x₁ + x₂) = F(x₁) + F(x₂), and homogeneity, F(ax) = aF(x). Many physical systems can be modeled as linear, which makes them easier to analyze with [[Fourier analysis|Fourier]] and [[Laplace transform|Laplace transforms]], though the principle is only approximately true of real systems. The total [[Electric field|electric field]] of several charges is the vector sum of their individual fields, and ordinary [[Light|light]] is described as a superposition of plane waves.

Belief or practice considered irrational or supernatural by non-practitioners. The term is commonly applied to beliefs about luck, fate, [[Magic (supernatural)|magic]], [[Astrology|astrology]], amulets, fortune telling and spirits, especially the belief that future events can be foretold by unrelated prior events. Superstitions are usually described as irrational beliefs at odds with scientific knowledge, and what counts as superstition varies across cultures and time. [[Cicero]] contrasted the Latin term superstitio with mainstream religion, arguing that religion is not destroyed by destroying superstition. In 1520, [[Martin Luther]] accused the popes of superstition. The word is also used for religions not practiced by a society's majority, and by antireligious critics for all religion.

Theoretical framework in [[Particle physics|particle physics]] proposing a symmetry between [[Boson|bosons]] and [[Fermion|fermions]]. Every known particle would have a partner, or superpartner, of the opposite type, with a spin differing by half an integer. In the simplest version, partners share the same mass; more complex theories break the symmetry so that partners differ in mass. If confirmed, supersymmetry could help explain [[Dark matter|dark matter]] and the hierarchy problem. A supersymmetric extension of the [[Standard Model]] is a candidate for physics beyond it, but none has been experimentally verified. Several experiments have failed to find evidence for it, and some physicists argue the theory is dead. Its mathematics has also been applied to nuclear physics, optics, statistical mechanics and cosmology.

[[Volcano]] whose eruption reached a volcanic explosivity index (VEI) of 8, the scale's maximum. Its deposits total more than 1,000 cubic kilometers. Pressure builds in a large magma pool until the [[Crust (geology)|crust]] ruptures, which can occur at hotspots such as Yellowstone or subduction zones such as Toba. Large-volume eruptions are often linked to large igneous provinces, such as the [[Siberian Traps]], which can cover huge areas with [[Lava|lava]] and cause long-lasting climate change. The Oruanui eruption of New Zealand's Taupō Volcano, about 25,600 years ago, was the most recent VEI-8 eruption. The term was popularized by the BBC program *Horizon* in 2000.

Economic model of price determination in a [[Market (economics)|market]]. In [[Microeconomics|microeconomics]], it holds that the price of a good in a perfectly competitive market settles where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. The concept forms the theoretical basis of modern economics. Under perfect competition, supply is determined by marginal cost: firms produce additional output while its cost is below the market price, and a rise in raw material costs shifts supply to the left. Where a firm has market power, as under a [[Monopoly|monopoly]] or oligopoly, a more complicated model is needed. In [[Macroeconomics|macroeconomics]], an aggregate demand–aggregate supply model describes total output and the price level. Alfred Marshall presented the framework in his 1890 *Principles of Economics*.

Group in which members provide each other with mostly nonprofessional help for a shared, usually burdensome, condition. Members share coping strategies, relate personal experiences and build a sense of community. Groups may meet in person, through newsletters or telephone chains, on [[Internet|internet]] forums, or exclusively online. Self-help groups are run by volunteers with personal experience, such as the twelve-step groups of Alcoholics Anonymous. Professionally facilitated groups, often found in [[Hospital|hospitals]] and treatment centers, are led by social workers or psychologists. Groups form around conditions from [[Grief|bereavement]] to [[Mental health|mental health]] problems. Since at least 1982, the internet has hosted support groups, and one study of head and neck cancer patients found that longer online participation was associated with better health-related quality of life.

headword: Supreme Court of the United States
sort_key: supreme court of the united states
entry: Highest court in the U.S. federal [[Judiciary|judiciary]]. It has ultimate appellate jurisdiction over federal cases and over state cases turning on constitutional or federal law. Its composition was set by the Judiciary Act of 1789. It now has nine justices, including the chief justice, who serve for life unless they retire, resign or are removed. The president appoints new justices with the advice and consent of the Senate. In 1803 the court asserted the power of judicial review, the ability to invalidate a [[Statute|statute]] for violating the Constitution. Each year it receives about 7,000 petitions for certiorari but grants about 80. The court sits in [[Washington, D.C.]]

Indian actress in Gujarati and Hindi films and television. She holds a bachelor's degree in fine arts, specializing in [[Bharatanatyam]], from the University of [[Mumbai]]. Her first film was Shyam Benegal's *Kalyug* (1981), an adaptation of the [[Mahabharata]], for which she won a Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actress. She is best known on television as Hansa Parekh in *Khichdi*. She has received three Filmfare Awards, the third for *Goliyon Ki Raasleela Ram-Leela* (2013). She also received an Indian Telly Award for her comic role in *Khichdi*.

Capital and largest city of East Java province, [[Indonesia]]. Indonesia's second-largest city after [[Jakarta]], it lies on the northeastern corner of [[Java]], on the Madura Strait. It is one of the earliest port cities in Southeast Asia and had 2,874,314 residents at the 2020 census, with over 10 million in its metropolitan area. The city was settled in the 10th century, and from the 18th century until the mid-20th century it was the largest city in the [[Dutch East Indies]]. Principal exports from its port include [[Tobacco|tobacco]], [[Coffee|coffee]] and sugar. Its founding date is 31 May 1293, when forces of the [[Majapahit]] kingdom clashed with those of [[Kublai Khan]]. The name is derived from a Javanese phrase meaning "bravely facing danger."

City on the Tapti River in [[Gujarat]], western India, near the [[Arabian Sea]]. Once a large seaport, it is now the commercial center of South Gujarat and the second-largest city in the state after [[Ahmedabad]]. About 90% of the world's diamonds are cut and polished there, and its textile industry is a major supplier of apparel and accessories. Under the [[Mughal Empire]] it was a major port, later hosting European factories from the British, Dutch and Portuguese. Surat was selected in 2015 for an [[IBM]] Smarter Cities Challenge grant and is one of twenty Indian cities developed under Prime Minister [[Narendra Modi]]'s flagship Smart Cities Mission. The Surat Diamond Bourse is the world's largest office building by floor area.

Energy per unit [[Area|area]] of a liquid's surface, equivalently a force per unit length. Cohesive forces pull surface molecules inward, so liquid surfaces tend to contract to the smallest possible area; this is why droplets form spheres. [[Water]] has a surface tension of 72.8 millinewtons per meter at 20 °C, high because of its [[Hydrogen bond|hydrogen bonds]]; this lets objects denser than water, such as razor blades and water striders, float. Surfactants such as [[Detergent|detergents]] reduce surface tension, allowing liquids to spread and contact other materials. The SI unit is the [[Newton (unit)|newton]] per meter. Mercury, where cohesion dominates, forms a convex meniscus in glass, while water forms a concave one.

Guided [[Missile|missile]] fired from ground or sea to destroy aircraft or other missiles. Developed during World War II but not operational then, surface-to-air missiles entered service in the second half of the 1950s and displaced most anti-aircraft guns. The American Nike Ajax was the first operational system; the Soviet Union's S-75 Dvina was the most produced. Guidance is typically by [[Radar|radar]], infrared or command. The Soviet SA-2 downed U.S. U-2 spy planes over the Soviet Union in 1960, during the [[Cold War]]. Modern examples include the Patriot and S-300 wide-area systems and the man-portable Stinger.
